expression: For {task}, existing methods remain limited by {specific constraint}.
meaning: Introduces a concrete research gap tied to a task and a named constraint.
guidance: Use only after verifying that the closest relevant methods share the stated constraint. Name the setting in which it matters.
avoid: Avoid replacing the constraint with 'limited performance' or implying that every prior method has the same weakness.
examples: For {task}, existing methods remain limited by {assumption} when {condition}.
In {setting}, current approaches require {resource or supervision}, which restricts {capability}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Our key insight is that {insight}, which enables {capability}.
meaning: States the conceptual observation that motivates the method and connects it to a scoped capability.
guidance: Express a technical relationship that the paper actually establishes or uses. Follow with the mechanism that realizes it.
avoid: Do not use 'key insight' for a restatement of the method name or an unsupported causal story.
examples: Our key insight is that {representation property} permits {operation}, which enables {capability}.
The central observation is that {condition}; this motivates {design choice}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: We introduce {method}, which {mechanism} to {objective}.
meaning: Names the contribution and summarizes its operative mechanism and objective in one sentence.
guidance: Replace the slots with the paper-level mechanism, not a list of low-level implementation details. Use the exact method name from the manuscript.
avoid: Avoid chaining several modules with 'novel' adjectives without explaining their function.
examples: We introduce {method}, which combines {mechanisms} to {objective}.
We develop {method}, a {method class} that {mechanism} for {task}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Across {evaluation scope}, {method} changes {metric} by {value} relative to {comparator}.
meaning: Reports one principal verified result with its evaluation scope, metric, magnitude, and comparator.
guidance: Specify whether the value is absolute, relative, or in percentage points. Use the same aggregation and comparison set as the referenced display.
avoid: Do not average incompatible tasks or select the largest favorable result while implying it summarizes the full study.
examples: Across {number} {tasks}, {method} improves {metric} by {value} percentage points over {comparator}.
Under {shift}, {method} reduces {error metric} from {baseline value} to {method value}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: These results support {scoped conclusion} under {evaluated conditions}.
meaning: Closes an empirical summary with a conclusion bounded by the actual evaluation.
guidance: Name the datasets, tasks, shifts, assumptions, or system conditions that bound the conclusion when they are material.
avoid: Avoid turning benchmark evidence into an unrestricted claim about real-world deployment or general intelligence.
examples: These results support {conclusion} for {task family} under {protocol}.
The evidence supports transfer across {held-out axis}, but does not establish {broader scope}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: This work studies {task} under {operational setting}.
meaning: Defines the paper's task and setting before broader motivation or method details.
guidance: Specify the decision, observation, data, interaction, or deployment regime that makes the task operationally distinct.
avoid: Avoid beginning from an expansive societal claim when the paper evaluates a narrower technical setting.
examples: This work studies {task} under {observation and action constraints}.
We consider {task} in the {offline, online, simulated, or real-system} setting.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Within {scope}, the closest approaches can be compared along {axis one} and {axis two}.
meaning: Organizes related approach families by explicit technical dimensions relevant to the present argument.
guidance: Choose verified axes such as representation, supervision, data, decision rule, interaction regime, or deployment assumption.
avoid: Do not manufacture a taxonomy that collapses technically heterogeneous work or omits the closest method.
examples: Within {task}, the closest approaches can be compared by how they represent {entity} and obtain {supervision}.
Existing methods can be distinguished by {decision mechanism} and {interaction regime}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: This assumption becomes restrictive when {condition}, because {consequence}.
meaning: Connects a verified method assumption to the condition under which it limits the target capability.
guidance: State the assumption, triggering condition, and consequence explicitly. Support literature and empirical claims with primary evidence.
avoid: Do not describe a design difference as restrictive without showing why it matters for the task.
examples: This assumption becomes restrictive when {shift}, because {technical consequence}.
The requirement for {resource} limits deployment in {setting}, where {constraint}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Motivated by this observation, we design {mechanism} to {goal}.
meaning: Bridges a stated insight or empirical observation to the paper's design response.
guidance: Ensure the antecedent observation directly motivates the mechanism. Name the technical goal rather than 'better performance.'
avoid: Avoid using the transition when the design choice is unrelated to the preceding limitation.
examples: Motivated by this observation, we design {mechanism} to preserve {property}.
This analysis motivates {design choice}, which targets {failure mode}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: The design addresses {challenge} by {technical choice}.
meaning: Maps one emphasized challenge to the corresponding design mechanism.
guidance: Use the same challenge and component names throughout the Introduction, Method, and experiments. Avoid implying causal sufficiency without evidence.
avoid: Do not introduce a challenge that no design element or experiment addresses.
examples: The design addresses {challenge} by conditioning {mechanism} on {signal}.
To handle {challenge}, the model uses {technical choice}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Our contributions are evaluated through {research questions}.
meaning: Frames empirical contributions as questions that the Experiments section is designed to answer.
guidance: Replace the slot with two or three concrete questions or evaluation axes. Pair non-empirical contributions with theorems, resources, or analyses instead.
avoid: Avoid treating the mere number of experiments as a contribution.
examples: We evaluate whether {method} improves {outcome}, transfers across {shift}, and reduces {resource}.
The experiments test {main comparison}, {mechanism claim}, and {deployment boundary}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: We focus on {scope}; {non-goal} remains outside the present study.
meaning: States an explicit boundary that prevents an overbroad reading of the contribution.
guidance: Use for a material assumption or non-goal, especially when motivation is broader than evaluation. Keep it consistent with Limitations.
avoid: Do not use a non-goal to dismiss a comparison or safety issue that is essential to the central claim.
examples: We focus on {evaluated setting}; transfer to {unseen setting} remains outside the present study.
Our analysis concerns {formal regime} and does not establish {broader guarantee}.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: We evaluate {method} on {tasks} using {metrics} under {protocol}.
meaning: Introduces the evaluation scope, outcome measures, and protocol in one compact sentence.
guidance: Name the actual tasks, principal metrics, split or evaluation regime, and any material simulation or deployment condition.
avoid: Avoid 'we conduct extensive experiments' without stating what questions or settings are evaluated.
examples: We evaluate {method} on {benchmarks} using {metrics} under a matched {budget}.
We evaluate in {simulation or real system} on {tasks}, reporting {metrics} under {protocol}.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Higher values of {metric} indicate {meaning}; results are averaged over {unit}.
meaning: Defines metric direction, interpretation, and the statistical unit used for aggregation.
guidance: Use 'lower' where appropriate and name whether the unit is task, scene, episode, trial, seed, or example.
avoid: Do not let readers infer whether a metric is a percentage, fraction, count, error, or normalized score.
examples: Higher values of {metric} indicate {capability}; results are averaged over {tasks} and then over {seeds}.
Lower {metric} indicates {meaning}; each value is averaged over {evaluation unit}.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: We report {statistic} over {number} independent {runs or seeds}.
meaning: States the aggregation statistic and number of independent repetitions.
guidance: Replace the statistical unit precisely and explain nested averaging when episodes or scenes occur within seeds. Name uncertainty separately.
avoid: Avoid 'averaged over multiple runs' when the count, independence, and dispersion are not given.
examples: We report the mean and standard deviation over {number} independent seeds.
Values are medians over {number} runs, with {interval} percentiles in parentheses.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Hyperparameters are selected on {validation set} using {criterion}.
meaning: Declares which data and objective selected hyperparameters or checkpoints.
guidance: State whether one configuration is shared across tasks and whether test or shifted conditions influenced selection.
avoid: Do not report test-optimal settings as if they were selected without access to test results.
examples: Hyperparameters are selected on {validation tasks} using {metric}, and the selected configuration is fixed for all test tasks.
We select the checkpoint with the highest {validation metric} before evaluating it once on {test set}.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: All methods use the same {resource budget}; remaining differences are {differences}.
meaning: States one controlled comparison resource while disclosing consequential factors that remain unmatched.
guidance: Name data, environment interaction, parameters, training compute, tuning, or evaluation budgets precisely. Do not imply full fairness from one matched resource.
avoid: Avoid the blanket phrase 'under fair settings' without listing matched and unmatched factors.
examples: All methods use the same {interaction budget}; model size and pretraining data differ as noted in {location}.
Training data are matched across methods, while {baseline} uses {additional resource}.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Baseline results are {rerun or sourced} using {implementation and version}.
meaning: Records whether baseline numbers were reproduced or taken from a source and identifies the implementation.
guidance: State code commit or release, consequential changes, tuning policy, and whether the reported protocol matches the present evaluation.
avoid: Do not mix rerun and copied numbers without labeling their provenance and compatibility.
examples: Baseline results are reproduced using the authors' {release} with {documented changes}.
Results marked with {symbol} are taken from {verified source}; all others are rerun under our protocol.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Each real-system condition is evaluated in {trials} trials, with success defined as {criterion}.
meaning: Defines the trial count and success criterion for a physical or deployed-system evaluation.
guidance: Also state reset procedure, intervention policy, trial independence, task allocation, and the denominator used for success rate.
avoid: Do not report a success percentage without the number and composition of physical trials.
examples: Each real-robot task is evaluated in {trials} trials, with success defined as {terminal condition}.
We conduct {number} trials per {task and object} pair and count an intervention as {outcome}.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Latency is measured on {hardware} with {precision, batch, and timing boundary}.
meaning: Defines the hardware and measurement boundary required to interpret latency.
guidance: State warm-up, synchronization, repeats, input shape, preprocessing, action decoding, and whether the value is model-only or end to end.
avoid: Do not compare latency across hardware or confuse batched throughput with single-sample latency.
examples: Latency is measured on {hardware} at {precision} and batch size {value}, including {timing boundary}.
End-to-end control latency includes {components} and is averaged over {repetitions} after {warm-up}.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: The {split} holds out {unit} from all training and selection data.
meaning: Defines a held-out unit and excludes it from both model fitting and selection.
guidance: Name whether the unit is subject, scene, object, task, environment, embodiment, or temporal block. Disclose any preprocessing learned globally.
avoid: Do not call a test condition unseen if it influenced prompts, hyperparameters, checkpoint selection, or data curation.
examples: The test split holds out {objects} from all training and validation trajectories.
For cross-environment evaluation, {environments} are excluded from both training and model selection.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: On {metric}, {method} changes {baseline value} to {method value}, an {absolute or relative} difference of {value}.
meaning: Reports both endpoint values and labels the comparison as absolute or relative.
guidance: For percentages, distinguish percentage-point differences from relative percent changes. Retain the metric unit and aggregation.
avoid: Avoid 'improves by 10%' when readers cannot tell whether this means ten percentage points or ten percent relative.
examples: On {metric}, {method} increases the score from {value} to {value}, a gain of {points} percentage points.
The error decreases from {value} to {value}, corresponding to a {relative value}% relative reduction.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: The advantage is consistent across {settings}, with {exceptions}.
meaning: Summarizes the breadth of an observed comparison while explicitly retaining exceptions.
guidance: Name the settings and define consistency using the direction, effect range, uncertainty, or success frequency. Fill the exception slot even if the answer is none observed.
avoid: Do not call a result consistent when only an average is positive or when important settings reverse the ranking.
examples: The advantage is consistent across {tasks}, except on {task}, where {outcome}.
The direction is stable over {seeds or scales}, although the magnitude varies from {range}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: The improvement is concentrated in {conditions}, whereas {other conditions} show {outcome}.
meaning: Identifies where an aggregate gain arises and contrasts it with conditions showing a different pattern.
guidance: Use subgroup or condition-level results that were defined or transparently labeled exploratory. Report denominators and uncertainty.
avoid: Do not select favorable subgroups post hoc without disclosure or ignore degradation elsewhere.
examples: The improvement is concentrated in {long-horizon tasks}, whereas {short-horizon tasks} show comparable performance.
Gains occur primarily under {shift}; in the reference condition, the methods differ by {value}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: This gain comes with {cost}, revealing a trade-off between {axes}.
meaning: Reports a measured benefit together with the resource, quality, safety, or robustness cost that accompanies it.
guidance: Quantify both axes under the same protocol and avoid causal language if the trade-off is only observational.
avoid: Do not hide the cost in a footnote while presenting the gain as unqualified superiority.
examples: This gain comes with {latency increase}, revealing a trade-off between {accuracy} and {deployment speed}.
Improved robustness is accompanied by {reference-condition change}, indicating a trade-off across {axes}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: We observe no consistent advantage on {scope}; the difference remains within {uncertainty}.
meaning: Reports a null or unstable comparison without converting it into evidence of equivalence.
guidance: Name the uncertainty statistic and comparison scope. If equivalence matters, use an appropriate equivalence or non-inferiority design.
avoid: Do not interpret a non-significant or noisy difference as proof that methods are identical.
examples: We observe no consistent advantage on {tasks}; differences vary in sign across {seeds}.
The estimate differs by {value}, with a {confidence interval} that includes {reference}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: This pattern is consistent with {hypothesis}, although {alternative} is not controlled.
meaning: Offers a mechanism interpretation while acknowledging a plausible uncontrolled explanation.
guidance: Use after stating the observed result. Replace the slots with a testable hypothesis and a concrete confounder or alternative mechanism.
avoid: Avoid 'this proves that the gain is due to' when the experiment does not identify the mechanism.
examples: This pattern is consistent with {mechanism}, although differences in {data or scale} are not controlled.
The result suggests {explanation}; however, {alternative} could also account for the change.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Variation across {seeds or trials} is {statistic}, indicating {bounded inference}.
meaning: Uses a named variability statistic to qualify the stability of an empirical result.
guidance: Name standard deviation, interquartile range, confidence interval, or another appropriate statistic and keep the inference modest.
avoid: Do not call a method stable from one run or from low variation over correlated evaluation episodes.
examples: Variation across seeds is {standard deviation}, indicating that the ranking is {stable or uncertain} under this protocol.
The interval across trials is {range}, so the observed difference should be interpreted as {bounded conclusion}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: The joint variant differs from the sum of individual changes, suggesting an interaction between {components}.
meaning: Describes non-additive ablation behavior as evidence consistent with a component interaction.
guidance: Use only when the factorial variants and common reference permit the comparison. Quantify the observed non-additivity and uncertainty.
avoid: Do not infer interaction from unrelated single-drop variants or unmatched optimization settings.
examples: The joint variant changes {metric} by {value}, compared with {individual effects}, suggesting an interaction between {components}.
The benefit of {component A} appears only with {component B}, consistent with their intended coupling.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Performance degrades under {condition}, which limits the claim to {scope}.
meaning: Connects an observed failure condition to the boundary it imposes on the paper's claim.
guidance: Quantify the degradation, state the denominator, and distinguish a sampled failure condition from a universal boundary.
avoid: Do not bury a condition that directly contradicts an Abstract or Introduction claim.
examples: Performance degrades under {shift}, which limits the claim to {evaluated range}.
Success falls from {value} to {value} for {condition}; we therefore restrict the conclusion to {scope}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Failure cases are dominated by {category}, accounting for {fraction} of {denominator}.
meaning: Reports a failure category with its frequency and explicit denominator.
guidance: Define a mutually interpretable failure taxonomy, label multi-cause cases, and state whether categories were assigned manually or automatically.
avoid: Do not select illustrative failures without reporting how frequently they occur in the evaluated population.
examples: Failure cases are dominated by {category}, accounting for {count} of {total} unsuccessful trials.
Among {denominator}, {fraction} involve {condition}; category labels were assigned using {procedure}.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Results on {dataset or task} under {protocol}. {Metric direction and units}.
meaning: Provides the first two functional sentences of a self-contained main-results caption.
guidance: Continue with aggregation, uncertainty, runs, emphasis, and protocol exceptions. Use the exact split and evaluation setting.
avoid: Do not use a one-phrase caption that forces readers to reconstruct the protocol from the prose.
examples: Results on {tasks} under the {split} protocol. Higher {metric} is better; values are {units} and report {statistic} over {runs}.
Evaluation on {environment} with {budget}. Lower {metric} is better, and bold marks the best comparable result.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Ablation of {components} with all variants trained under {matched protocol}.
meaning: Introduces an ablation caption and states the matched condition needed to compare variants.
guidance: Define component indicators, full-model row, metric, runs, uncertainty, and any retuning policy in the remaining caption.
avoid: Do not claim a matched ablation when variants use different data, budgets, selection, or evaluation.
examples: Ablation of {components} with all variants trained under the same {data and compute budget}. Values report {statistic} over {seeds}.
Component analysis on {task}; the full model is {row}, and each variant changes {factor}.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Generalization from {training condition} to {held-out condition}.
meaning: Names the training and held-out conditions at the start of a generalization-table caption.
guidance: Continue with the held-out unit, selection protocol, metrics, runs, uncertainty, and reference condition.
avoid: Do not use 'unseen' without specifying what was withheld and whether it influenced model selection.
examples: Generalization from {training environments} to held-out {environments}. Test environments are excluded from training and validation.
Transfer from {embodiments} to unseen {embodiments}; success rates are averaged over {trials}.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Quality and deployment cost measured under {hardware and timing protocol}.
meaning: Frames an efficiency caption around both outcome quality and a reproducibly measured deployment resource.
guidance: Name hardware, precision, batch, input, warm-up, timing boundary, repeats, resource units, and metric directions.
avoid: Do not label a table efficiency when it reports only parameter count or latency without task quality.
examples: Quality and deployment cost measured on {hardware} at {precision} and batch size {value}. Latency includes {boundary}.
Task success and control latency under {deployment protocol}; values report {statistic} over {repeats}.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: Sensitivity to {parameter}; {default marker} denotes the selected configuration.
meaning: Introduces a sensitivity caption and identifies the configuration used elsewhere in the paper.
guidance: State the full range, selection data and objective, fixed factors, runs, uncertainty, and changed resource when scale varies.
avoid: Do not show only values near the chosen optimum or imply a scaling law from a narrow sweep.
examples: Sensitivity to {parameter}; the dagger denotes the validation-selected configuration. All other settings and seeds are fixed.
Scaling with {data or model size}; bold identifies the configuration used for the main experiments, not an oracle test optimum.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

expression: A dash denotes an unreported value, not a measured zero.
meaning: Separates missing or unreported results from numeric zero and from conditions that are not applicable.
guidance: Define every symbol in the caption or footnote. Use 0 or 0.0 only for a measured zero and N/A only when the metric or condition does not apply.
avoid: Do not encode unavailable, failed, and zero-valued results with the same blank cell or dash.
examples: A dash denotes a result that was not reported; N/A indicates that the metric is not applicable.
Zero is reported numerically, while failed runs are counted under {failure policy}.

provenance.note: Original table-reporting guidance authored after the section-writing audit.
